# Definition of f-compatibility

::: {#def-f-compatibility .callout-important icon="false"}
## (f-compatibility on k-copy)
Given $K$ observables $\{A_1,\ldots,A_K\}$ on outcome sets $\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_K\}$ with distribution vector family $(\vec{p}_1,\ldots,\vec{p}_n)$.
Suppose $\mathcal{F}:=\{f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}}$ is a class of functions of probability vector family $(\vec{p}_1,\ldots,\vec{p}_n)$.
 We say that $\{A_i\}$ is $k$-copy $\mathcal{F}$-compatible if there exists a POVM $\{\Pi_j\}_{j \in \mathcal{J}}$ on $\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}$ and classical functions $\{h_\alpha: \mathcal{J} \to \mathbb{R}\}$ such that
$$
f_\alpha\big(\vec{p}_1(\rho),\ldots,\vec{p}_n(\rho)\big) = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} h_\alpha(j)\;\mathrm{tr}[\Pi_j\;\rho^{\otimes k}], \quad \forall\,\rho,\;\forall\,\alpha
$$
We denote $k(\mathcal{F})$ as the smallest copy number such that $\{A_1,\ldots,A_K\}$ is $\mathcal{F}$-compatible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="false"}
## Discussion

- When $f_\alpha$ is the projection to the $i$-th observable's $a_i$-th outcome probability, i.e., $f_{(i,a_i)}(\vec{p}_1,\ldots,\vec{p}_n) = p_i(a_i) = \mathrm{tr}[A_i^{a_i}\rho]$ for **all $i$ and all $a_i$**, it requires extracting the probability of each outcome of each observable from the statistics of $\{\Pi_j\}$. This is **equivalent to** the original definition of $k$-compatible.
- We see that $\mathcal{F} = \{f_{(i,a_i)}\}_{i=1}^K$ must contains largest copy number $k(\{f_{(i,a_i)}\}_{i=1}^K)$ compared to others $k(\mathcal{F}), \forall \mathcal{F} \neq \{f_{(i,a_i)}\}_{i=1}^K$.

:::

**Examples:** $\{X,Y,Z\}$.

In the case $A_i$ has 2-outcome $+1,-1$ (like Pauli observable), we can set $p_i(\rho):= \mathrm{tr}[A_i(+1)\rho]$. Then the functional reduced to a function:
$$
f_\alpha\big(\vec{p}_1(\rho),\ldots,\vec{p}_n(\rho)\big) = f_\alpha\big(p_1,\ldots,p_n\big)
$$

If we take set take $X,Y,Z$ and:

- Further setup $$ \begin{aligned}f_1(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= (2p_x-1)^2, \\f_2(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= (2p_y-1)^2, \\f_3(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= (2p_z-1)^2\end{aligned},$$ this reduced to the case of estimates $\{|\mathrm{tr}(X\rho)|^2, |\mathrm{tr}(Y\rho)|^2, |\mathrm{tr}(Z\rho)|^2\}$ with a unified measurement setting.
- Further setup $$ \begin{aligned}f_1(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= p_x, \\f_2(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= p_y, \\f_3(p_x,p_y,p_z) &= p_z\end{aligned},$$ this reduced to the case (i). estimates $\{\mathrm{tr}(X\rho), \mathrm{tr}(Y\rho), \mathrm{tr}(Z\rho)\}$ with a unified measurement setting or (ii). implement three measurement settings $X,Y,Z$ simultaneously.


As shown in previous [post](./compatibility.html), compatiability problem can be reduced to a SDP problem. We can also reduce f-compatibility problem to a SDP problem either, as described in the following theorem.
We noted that the only difference compared to [post](./compatibility.html) is the relax of condition marginal of parent POVMs recovers each compatiable measurement to an $|s_i| < 1$ estimator based on parent POVMs

### Linearization via k-copy lifting

The key observation enabling an SDP formulation is that polynomial functionals of outcome probabilities become **linear** when lifted to $k$-copy states. Since $p_i(\rho) = \mathrm{tr}[A_i^{(+)}\rho]$, any monomial of degree $k$ satisfies:
$$
p_{i_1}(\rho)\cdots p_{i_k}(\rho) = \mathrm{tr}\bigl[(A_{i_1}^{(+)}\otimes \cdots \otimes A_{i_k}^{(+)})\;\rho^{\otimes k}\bigr].
$$
Therefore, any degree-$k$ polynomial $f_\alpha(p_1,\ldots,p_K)$ can be written as
$$
f_\alpha\bigl(\vec{p}(\rho)\bigr) = \mathrm{tr}[F_\alpha\;\rho^{\otimes k}],
$$ {#eq-linearization}
where $F_\alpha \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})$ is a Hermitian operator determined by the polynomial structure of $f_\alpha$ and the POVM elements $\{A_i^{(a)}\}$.

### f-Compatibility SDP

:::{#thm-f-compatibility-SDP .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem (f-Compatibility SDP)
Let $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^K$ be observables on $\mathcal{H}$ and $\mathcal{F} = \{f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a class of polynomial functionals of degree at most $k$ in the outcome probabilities. Define the $k$-copy linearization $F_\alpha \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})$ via @eq-linearization. Then $\{A_i\}$ is $k$-copy $\mathcal{F}$-compatible if and only if the following SDP is feasible:
$$
\boxed{
\begin{align*}
\text{Find:} \quad & \{\Pi_j\}_{j \in \mathcal{J}},\; \{h_\alpha(j)\}_{\alpha,j} \\
\text{Subject to:} \quad & \sum_{j} h_\alpha(j)\,\Pi_j = F_\alpha \quad \forall\,\alpha \in \mathcal{A} \\
& \sum_{j} \Pi_j = \mathbb{I}^{\otimes k} \\
& \Pi_j \geq 0 \quad \forall\,j \\
& |h_\alpha(j)| \leq 1 \quad \forall\,\alpha,j
\end{align*}
}
$$
The **robustness of f-incompatibility** is $r^* = s^* - 1$, where $s^*$ is the optimum of:
$$
\boxed{
\begin{align*}
\text{Minimize:} \quad & s \\
\text{Subject to:} \quad & \sum_{j} h_\alpha(j)\,\Pi_j = F_\alpha \quad \forall\,\alpha \in \mathcal{A} \\
& \sum_{j} \Pi_j = s\,\mathbb{I}^{\otimes k} \\
& \Pi_j \geq 0 \quad \forall\,j \\
& |h_\alpha(j)| \leq 1 \quad \forall\,\alpha,j
\end{align*}
}
$$ {#eq-f-compat-primal}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (f-Compatibility SDP)

**($\Leftarrow$: Feasibility implies f-compatibility.)** Given a feasible solution $\{\Pi_j, h_\alpha(j)\}$ with $s=1$, for any state $\rho$:
$$
\sum_j h_\alpha(j)\,\mathrm{tr}[\Pi_j\,\rho^{\otimes k}] = \mathrm{tr}\!\left[\sum_j h_\alpha(j)\Pi_j\;\rho^{\otimes k}\right] = \mathrm{tr}[F_\alpha\,\rho^{\otimes k}] = f_\alpha(\vec{p}(\rho)),
$$
which is precisely the f-compatibility condition of @def-f-compatibility.

**($\Rightarrow$: f-compatibility implies feasibility.)** Suppose $\{A_i\}$ is $k$-copy $\mathcal{F}$-compatible via POVM $\{\Pi_j\}$ and estimators $\{h_\alpha(j)\}$. Then for all $\rho$:
$$
\mathrm{tr}\!\left[\left(\sum_j h_\alpha(j)\Pi_j - F_\alpha\right)\rho^{\otimes k}\right] = 0.
$$
Since this holds for all $\rho$ (and hence for all $\rho^{\otimes k}$ which span the symmetric subspace, and $F_\alpha$ is symmetric), we obtain the operator identity $\sum_j h_\alpha(j)\Pi_j = F_\alpha$. The POVM conditions $\Pi_j \geq 0$ and $\sum_j \Pi_j = \mathbb{I}^{\otimes k}$ hold by definition.

**Connection to standard compatibility:** When $f_\alpha = p_i$ (linear functionals extracting individual outcome probabilities), we have $F_\alpha = A_i^{(+)}$ and $k=1$. The estimator condition $\sum_j h_i(j)\Pi_j = A_i^{(+)}$ with $|h_i(j)|\leq 1$ is equivalent to the marginal condition of standard joint measurability (see the Pauli Compatibility Problem below).

**Connection to inhomogeneous SDP [@skrzypczyk2019all]:** The robustness version with super-normalization $s > 1$ parallels the inhomogeneous compatibility robustness SDP. The inequality $\geq$ in the standard SDP (requiring marginals to dominate each measurement) is replaced by the exact estimator condition with bounded coefficients $|h_\alpha(j)| \leq 1$.
:::

### Dual Problem

:::{#lem-f-compatibility-dual .callout-note icon="false"}
## Lemma (f-Compatibility Dual)
The dual of the f-compatibility robustness SDP (@eq-f-compat-primal) is:
$$
\boxed{
\begin{align*}
\text{Maximize:} \quad & \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{tr}[\Lambda_\alpha\, F_\alpha] \\
\text{Subject to:} \quad & \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}} |\Lambda_\alpha| \leq W \\
& \mathrm{tr}[W] = 1 \\
& W \geq 0, \quad \Lambda_\alpha \text{ Hermitian}
\end{align*}
}
$$ {#eq-f-compat-dual}
where $|\Lambda_\alpha| = \sqrt{\Lambda_\alpha^\dagger \Lambda_\alpha}$ denotes the operator absolute value.

Equivalently, eliminating $W$, the dual reduces to:
$$
\text{Maximize:}\; \sum_{\alpha} \mathrm{tr}[\Lambda_\alpha F_\alpha], \quad \text{s.t.}\; \sum_{\alpha} \mathrm{tr}[|\Lambda_\alpha|] \leq 1.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Dual Derivation)

We reformulate the primal by introducing $\Gamma_{\alpha,j} := h_\alpha(j)\,\Pi_j$. The bounded estimator condition $|h_\alpha(j)| \leq 1$ becomes $-\Pi_j \leq \Gamma_{\alpha,j} \leq \Pi_j$, i.e., $\Pi_j \pm \Gamma_{\alpha,j} \geq 0$. The primal becomes:
$$
\begin{align*}
\text{Minimize:} \quad & s \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_j \Gamma_{\alpha,j} = F_\alpha, \quad \forall\,\alpha \\
& \sum_j \Pi_j = s\,\mathbb{I}^{\otimes k} \\
& \Pi_j + \Gamma_{\alpha,j} \geq 0, \quad \Pi_j - \Gamma_{\alpha,j} \geq 0, \quad \forall\,\alpha,j
\end{align*}
$$

Introduce Lagrange multipliers: Hermitian $\Lambda_\alpha$ for the estimator constraints, Hermitian $W$ for normalization, and PSD matrices $U^+_{\alpha,j}, U^-_{\alpha,j} \geq 0$ for the bounded-estimator constraints. The Lagrangian is:
$$
\begin{align*}
L &= s + \sum_\alpha \mathrm{tr}\!\left[\Lambda_\alpha\!\left(F_\alpha - \sum_j \Gamma_{\alpha,j}\right)\right] + \mathrm{tr}\!\left[W\!\left(\sum_j \Pi_j - s\,\mathbb{I}\right)\right] \\
& \quad - \sum_{\alpha,j}\mathrm{tr}[U^+_{\alpha,j}(\Pi_j + \Gamma_{\alpha,j})] - \sum_{\alpha,j}\mathrm{tr}[U^-_{\alpha,j}(\Pi_j - \Gamma_{\alpha,j})]
\end{align*}
$$

Collecting terms by primal variables:

- **Coefficient of $s$:** $1 - \mathrm{tr}[W] = 0 \implies \mathrm{tr}[W] = 1$.
- **Coefficient of $\Pi_j$:** $W - \sum_\alpha(U^+_{\alpha,j} + U^-_{\alpha,j}) = 0$, so $W = \sum_\alpha(U^+_{\alpha,j} + U^-_{\alpha,j})$ for each $j$.
- **Coefficient of $\Gamma_{\alpha,j}$:** $-\Lambda_\alpha - U^+_{\alpha,j} + U^-_{\alpha,j} = 0$, so $\Lambda_\alpha = U^-_{\alpha,j} - U^+_{\alpha,j}$.

From the last condition: $U^+_{\alpha,j} + U^-_{\alpha,j} \geq |U^-_{\alpha,j} - U^+_{\alpha,j}| = |\Lambda_\alpha|$ (since $U^\pm \geq 0$ implies $U^+ + U^- \geq |U^+ - U^-|$). Summing over $\alpha$:
$$
W = \sum_\alpha (U^+_{\alpha,j} + U^-_{\alpha,j}) \geq \sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha|.
$$
The tightest bound is achieved when $U^+_{\alpha,j} = (|\Lambda_\alpha| - \Lambda_\alpha)/2$ and $U^-_{\alpha,j} = (|\Lambda_\alpha| + \Lambda_\alpha)/2$ (independent of $j$), giving $W = \sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha|$.

The dual objective is $\sum_\alpha \mathrm{tr}[\Lambda_\alpha F_\alpha]$ with constraints $\sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha| \leq W$, $\mathrm{tr}[W]=1$, $W \geq 0$.

Since we maximize over $W$ subject to $W \geq \sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha|$ and $\mathrm{tr}[W]=1$, the optimal $W^* = \sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha|$ (when $\mathrm{tr}[\sum_\alpha |\Lambda_\alpha|] \leq 1$), yielding the simplified form $\sum_\alpha \mathrm{tr}[|\Lambda_\alpha|] \leq 1$.
:::

This SDP can be solved analytically for some cases. Here we take an well known example.
We know that given a set of Pauli obsevables $\{P_i\}_i$, getting its average is as hard as compatiable realization of $\frac{\mathbb{I} \pm P_i}{2}$

:::{#the-Pauli-compatibility-problem .callout-important icon="false"}
## The Pauli Compatibility Problem
Given a set of Pauli obsevables $\{P_i\}_i$, getting its average is as hard as compatiable realization of $\frac{\mathbb{I} \pm P_i}{2}$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

We show that for two-outcome Pauli observables, f-compatibility with **bounded estimators** ($|h_i(j)|\leq 1$) for the linear functionals $f_i(\vec{p}) = \mathrm{tr}[P_i\rho]$ is **equivalent** to standard joint measurability of $\{M_i^{\pm} = \frac{\mathbb{I}\pm P_i}{2}\}$.

**($\Leftarrow$: Compatibility $\Rightarrow$ estimation.)** Suppose $\{M_i^+, M_i^-\}_{i=1}^K$ are jointly measurable. By definition there exists a parent POVM $\{G_\lambda\}_\lambda$ and conditional distributions $p(a|i,\lambda)$ with $a \in \{+1,-1\}$ such that:
$$
\frac{\mathbb{I} + a\, P_i}{2} = \sum_\lambda p(a|i,\lambda)\, G_\lambda, \quad \forall\, a, i.
$$
Taking the difference $a=+1$ minus $a=-1$:
$$
P_i = \sum_\lambda \bigl[p(+1|i,\lambda) - p(-1|i,\lambda)\bigr]\, G_\lambda =: \sum_\lambda h_i(\lambda)\, G_\lambda.
$$
Since $p(+1|i,\lambda) + p(-1|i,\lambda) = 1$ and both are non-negative, $|h_i(\lambda)| \leq 1$. Therefore $\mathrm{tr}[P_i\rho] = \sum_\lambda h_i(\lambda)\,\mathrm{tr}[G_\lambda\rho]$ for all $\rho$, which is exactly f-compatibility with bounded estimators.

**($\Rightarrow$: Estimation $\Rightarrow$ compatibility.)** Suppose there exists a POVM $\{\Pi_j\}_j$ and estimators $\{h_i(j)\}$ with $|h_i(j)| \leq 1$ such that $\sum_j h_i(j)\,\Pi_j = P_i$ for all $i$. Define conditional probabilities:
$$
p(\pm 1|i,j) := \frac{1 \pm h_i(j)}{2}.
$$
Since $|h_i(j)|\leq 1$, both $p(+1|i,j) \geq 0$ and $p(-1|i,j) \geq 0$, and they sum to 1. Now verify the marginals:
$$
\sum_j p(\pm 1|i,j)\,\Pi_j = \frac{1}{2}\sum_j \Pi_j \pm \frac{1}{2}\sum_j h_i(j)\,\Pi_j = \frac{\mathbb{I} \pm P_i}{2} = M_i^{\pm}.
$$
This is precisely a joint measurement realization of $\{M_i^+, M_i^-\}_{i=1}^K$ with parent POVM $\{\Pi_j\}$.
:::

We all know that $\{X,Y,Z\}$ measurement is not compatible, even on the 2-replica case, as shown in [this post](/theory/Posts/compatibility/multicopy_compatiability.html).
However, in the 2-replica case, the squared expectation value $|\mathrm{tr}(P_i\rho)|^2$ is f-compatible, as $P_i \otimes P_i$ commute with each other.
Note that the problem to get $\{|\mathrm{tr}(P_i\rho)|^2\}_i$ rather than implement measurement $\frac{\mathbb{I} \pm P_i}{2}$ means that we count the f-compatibility problem rather than the compatibility problem.
Using the SDP formulation of f-compatibility in the previous section, we can explain this analytically.

:::{#prop-bell-f-compat .callout-important icon="false"}
## Proposition (Bell Measurement Solves Squared-Expectation f-Compatibility)
For Pauli observables $\{X,Y,Z\}$ with functionals $f_i(\vec{p}) = |\mathrm{tr}(P_i\rho)|^2$ ($i=1,2,3$), the Bell measurement on $\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2}$ achieves exact $\mathcal{F}$-compatibility with $k=2$ and robustness $s^*=1$ (i.e., $r^*=0$).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

**Step 1: k-copy linearization.** Since $\mathrm{tr}[P_i\rho] = 2p_i - 1$, the squared expectation value satisfies:
$$
|\mathrm{tr}(P_i\rho)|^2 = \mathrm{tr}[P_i\rho]^2 = \mathrm{tr}\bigl[(P_i \otimes P_i)\,\rho^{\otimes 2}\bigr],
$$
so $F_i = P_i \otimes P_i \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2})$ and $k=2$.

**Step 2: Mutual commutativity.** For distinct Paulis $P_i, P_j$ (which anticommute: $P_iP_j = -P_jP_i$):
$$
[P_i \otimes P_i,\; P_j \otimes P_j] = (P_iP_j)\otimes(P_iP_j) - (P_jP_i)\otimes(P_jP_i) = (-P_jP_i)\otimes(-P_jP_i) - (P_jP_i)\otimes(P_jP_i) = 0.
$$
Hence $\{X\otimes X,\; Y\otimes Y,\; Z\otimes Z\}$ are mutually commuting Hermitian operators with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ and can be simultaneously diagonalized.

**Step 3: Joint eigenbasis is the Bell basis.** Direct computation gives the eigenvalues $(XX, YY, ZZ)$ for each Bell state:

| Bell state | $X\otimes X$ | $Y\otimes Y$ | $Z\otimes Z$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}$ | $+1$ | $-1$ | $+1$ |
| $|\Phi^-\rangle = \frac{|00\rangle-|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}$ | $-1$ | $+1$ | $+1$ |
| $|\Psi^+\rangle = \frac{|01\rangle+|10\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}$ | $+1$ | $+1$ | $-1$ |
| $|\Psi^-\rangle = \frac{|01\rangle-|10\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ |

**Step 4: SDP feasibility.** Set the Bell measurement POVM $\Pi_j = |B_j\rangle\langle B_j|$ ($j=1,\ldots,4$) and define estimators $h_i(j)$ as the eigenvalue of $P_i \otimes P_i$ at Bell state $|B_j\rangle$. Verify all constraints of @thm-f-compatibility-SDP:

- **Estimator condition:** $\sum_j h_i(j)\,\Pi_j = P_i\otimes P_i = F_i$ by spectral decomposition. $\checkmark$
- **Normalization:** $\sum_j \Pi_j = \mathbb{I}^{\otimes 2}$ (Bell states form a complete basis), with $s=1$. $\checkmark$
- **Positivity:** $\Pi_j = |B_j\rangle\langle B_j| \geq 0$. $\checkmark$
- **Bounded estimators:** $|h_i(j)| = 1 \leq 1$ (eigenvalues of Pauli tensor products are $\pm 1$). $\checkmark$

All constraints are satisfied with $s=1$. The f-compatibility robustness is $r^* = s^* - 1 = 0$: **no noise penalty is needed**.

**Contrast with standard compatibility.** Standard 2-copy compatibility of $\{X,Y,Z\}$ requires recovering the full marginal distributions $\frac{\mathbb{I}\pm a P_i}{2}$. This demands the lifted operators $\mathbb{I}\otimes P_i + P_i \otimes \mathbb{I}$ to be jointly accessible, but these do **not** commute for different $i$. From the [multicopy compatibility analysis](/theory/Posts/compatibility/multicopy_compatiability.html), the maximum sharpness parameter is $a_{\max} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} < 1$, so $\{X,Y,Z\}$ are **not** 2-compatible in the standard sense.

The essential difference: standard compatibility requires linear functionals of $\rho$ (involving $\mathbb{I}\otimes P_i + P_i\otimes\mathbb{I}$), while f-compatibility with squared expectations only needs quadratic functionals that become linear on $\rho^{\otimes 2}$ (involving $P_i\otimes P_i$), and these happen to commute.
:::
